'''''Pinus radiata''''' ([[synonym (taxonomy)|syn.]] ''Pinus insignis''), the '''Monterey pine''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17}}</ref> '''insignis pine'''<ref>{{cite book |display-authors=1 |author1=Kershner, Bruce |author2=Moore, Gerry |author3=Tufts, Craig |author4=Mathews, Daniel |author5=Nelson, Gil |author6=Spellenberg, Richard |author7=Thieret, John W. |author8=Purinton, Terry |author9=Block, Andrew |title=National Wildlife Federation Field Guide to Trees of North America |publisher=Sterling |location=New York |year=2008 |page=84 |isbn=978-1-4027-3875-3}}</ref> or '''radiata pine''', is a species of [[pine]] native to the [[Central Coast (California)|Central Coast]] of [[California]], and the [[Guadalupe Island|Guadalupe]] and [[Cedros Island|Cedros]] islands of [[Mexico]]. It is an [[evergreen]] [[conifer]] in the family [[Pinaceae]].

''Pinus radiata'' is a versatile, fast-growing, medium-density softwood, suitable for a wide range of uses and valued for rapid growth (up to two meters (6.5 feet) in one year),<ref>{{cite book | last= Edlin | first= Herbert L. | date= 1976 |title= Natural History of Trees | location= London | publisher= Weidenfeld & Nicolson | page= 33 }}</ref> as well as desirable [[lumber]] and [[Pulp (paper)|pulp]] qualities.<ref name=Mead>{{cite book|last=Mead|first=D|title=Sustainable management of Pinus radiata|year=2013|publisher=Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations|location=Rome|isbn=978-92-5-107634-7|url=http://www.fao.org/docrep/018/i3274e/i3274e00.htm}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-12-03 |title=Assessing & Managing Mid-rotation Wood Quality In Australian Softwood Plantations |url=https://fwpa.com.au/report/assessing-managing-mid-rotation-wood-quality-in-australian-softwood-plantations/ |access-date=2025-02-06 |website= |language=en-AU}}</ref> Its [[silviculture]] reflects a century of research, observation and practice.<ref name="Mead" /> It is often considered a model for growers of other plantation species.<ref name="Mead" />

Although ''P. radiata'' is extensively cultivated as a [[plantation timber]] in many [[temperateness|temperate]] parts of the world,<ref name="Gymnospermdatabase">{{Gymnosperm Database |family=Pinaceae |genus=Pinus |species=radiata}}</ref> it faces serious threats in its natural range,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.1hope.org/NativeMontereyPineStatus.pdf|title=Status of Native Monterey Pine (Pinus radiata) Ecosystems}}</ref> due to the introduction of a fungal parasite, the pine pitch canker (''[[Fusarium circinatum]]''). The pine shoot moth ''[[Rhyacionia buoliana]]'' is another serious problem. In cultivation in [[New Zealand]], ''Pinus radiata'' has grown as much as {{cvt|61|m}} in 41 years,<ref>{{ cite book | last= Duncalf | first= William G. | date= 1976 | title= Guinness Book of Plant Facts and Feats | location= Enfield, England | publisher= Guinness Superlatives Ltd | page= 78}}</ref> an average of {{cvt|1.5|m}} per year.

==Description==
[[File:Pinus radiata cone.jpg|thumb|Ovulate cone]]
[[File:Pinus radiata pollen cones, 2 cm scale bar.png|thumb|Pollen cones, 2 cm scale bar]]
''Pinus radiata'' is a [[pinophyta|coniferous]] [[evergreen]] tree growing to {{convert|15|-|30|m|-1|abbr=on}} tall in the wild, but up to {{convert|60|m|abbr=on}} in cultivation in optimum conditions, with upward pointing branches and a rounded top. The [[leaf|leaves]] ("needles") are bright green, in clusters of three (two in var. ''binata''), slender, {{convert|8|-|15|cm|frac=2|abbr=on}} long and with a blunt tip. The ovulate [[conifer cone|cones]] are {{convert|7|-|17|cm|in|frac=2|abbr=on}} long, brown, ovoid (egg-shaped), and usually set asymmetrically on a branch, attached at an oblique angle. The [[Bark (botany)|bark]] is fissured and dark gray to brown. When not cut short by disease or harvesting, it has a lifespan of 80 to 90 years.{{Citation needed|date=April 2021}}

The specific epithet ''radiata'' refers to the cracks which radiate from the umbo of the cone scales.<ref name="Powell" />

It is closely related to [[bishop pine]] and [[knobcone pine]], hybridizing readily with both species; it is distinguished from the former by needles in threes (not pairs), and from both by the cones not having a sharp spine on the scales.<ref name="Lanner">{{cite book | last=Lanner | first=Ronald M. | title=Conifers of California | publisher=Cachuma Press | publication-place=Los Olives, Calif | date=1999 | isbn=0-9628505-3-5 | page=}}</ref>

The modern plantation tree is vastly different from the native tree of Monterey.<ref name="Powell">{{cite book|last1=Powell|first1=Leslie|title=The Genus Pinus: A Reference Guide for Pines|date=9 February 2017|publisher=lulu.com|isbn=978-1365157172|page=112}}{{self-published source|date=April 2021}}</ref>{{self-published inline|date=February 2020}} In plantations the tree is commonly planted at 4 square meter spacing on a wide variety of landscapes from flat to moderately steep hills.<ref name="Powell" /> Because of selective breeding and more recently the extensive use of growth factor seedlings, forests planted since the 1990s have very straight tall trunks without the problem of twin leaders.<ref name="Powell" /> The trees are pruned in three [[Pruning#Crown raising|lifts]] so that the lower two-thirds of a mature tree is free of branches and hence of knots.<ref name="Powell" />

==Distribution and habitat==
In the United States, it is native to three very limited areas located in [[Santa Cruz County, California|Santa Cruz]], [[Monterey County, California|Monterey]], and [[San Luis Obispo County, California|San Luis Obispo]] Counties of California.<ref name=feis>{{cite web|url=https://www.fs.usda.gov/database/feis/plants/tree/pinrad/all.html#DISTRIBUTION%20AND%20OCCURRENCE|title=Pinus radiata|work=Fire Effects Information System|publisher=US Forest Service|access-date=2023-09-24|year=1993|first=Amy B|last=Cope}}</ref>

In Mexico, it is found on two islands in the Pacific Ocean, Guadalupe Island and Cedros Island.<ref name=feis/> 

On Guadalupe Island, located {{Cvt|280|km|nmi|round=5}} off the mainland coast, the pines are found on the steep northern end of the island, at elevations of around {{Cvt|500|to|1200|m}}, where they follow the ridgetops and steep slopes.<ref name="Rogers2005" /> [[Edward Palmer (botanist)|Edward Palmer]] and [[Francesco Franceschi (horticulturist)|Francescho Franceschi]] were the first to discover the pines on Guadalupe Island. When Franceschi visited in 1892, he noted that they extended all over the northern and northwestern part of the island, comprising a very thick forest, with some of the finest trees growing with the [[Brahea edulis|Guadalupe palm]].<ref name="Moran1996">{{Cite book |last=Moran|first=Reid|title=The Flora of Guadalupe Island|publisher=California Academy of Sciences|year=1996|isbn=0-940228-40-8|pages=62-65}}</ref>

On Cedros Island, the pines are more abundant, being found in far greater numbers partly due to the lack of [[feral goat]]s. (Goats were exterminated on Guadalupe island by 2007.) They are found at lower elevations than on Guadalupe, at around {{Cvt|285|to|690|m}}, on the windward ridges and canyons of the north and central parts of the island. In both cases, the pines seem to be heavily dependent on locations with a high frequency of [[fog]].<ref name="Rogers2005">{{Citation |last1=Rogers |first1=Deborah L. |chapter=Conserving the Pines of Guadalupe and Cedros Islands, Mexico: An International Collaboration |date=2005 |chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1007/1-4020-3774-0_2 |title=Environmental Issues in Latin America and the Caribbean |pages=31–54 |editor-last=Romero |editor-first=Aldemaro |place=Dordrecht |publisher=Springer Netherlands |language=en |doi=10.1007/1-4020-3774-0_2 |isbn=978-1-4020-3774-0 |access-date=2022-07-21 |last2=Jesús Vargas Hernández |first2=J. |last3=Matheson |first3=A. Colin |last4=Guerra Santos |first4=Jesús J. |editor2-last=West |editor2-first=Sarah E.|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref>

In Australia, New Zealand, and Spain it is the leading introduced tree<ref>Scott, C. W. 1960. Pinus radiata. Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, Forestry and Forest Products Study 14. Rome, Italy. 328 p. cited in {{harvnb|McDonald|Laacke|1990}}.</ref> and in Argentina, Chile, Uruguay, Kenya, and South Africa it is a major plantation species. It is also an [[Sandy Point, Tristan da Cunha|introduced tree]] on the world's most remote inhabited island, [[Tristan da Cunha]].{{Citation needed|date=April 2021}}

== Taxonomy ==

=== Subdivisions ===
Two [[Variety (botany)|varieties]] of this species have been recognized, each corresponding to the island they are endemic to in [[Baja California]]. Some authors [[Lumpers and splitters|lump]] these taxa and do not recognize [[Infraspecific name|infraspecies]].<ref name="rebman">{{Cite journal |last1=Rebman |first1=J. P. |last2=Gibson |first2=J. |last3=Rich |first3=K. |date=2016 |title=Annotated checklist of the vascular plants of Baja California, Mexico |url=http://sdplantatlas.org/pdffiles/BajaChecklist2016.pdf |journal=San Diego Society of Natural History |volume=45 |pages=131}}</ref>

On both islands it is the only pine species, and one of the few tree species. Compared to the mainland species, which are mostly three-needled, the insular varieties have their needles in bundles of two. Their cones are also smaller, and they show greater wind resistance in regards to wind-induced toppling.<ref name="Rogers2005" /> 

[[John Thomas Howell]] found that in some examples of the pines on Guadalupe Island, vigorous shoots often had needles in threes, similar to typical ''Pinus radiata''. Howell treated the pines on Guadalupe as three separate forms rather than the endemic variety, with forma ''radiata'' having very asymmetrical cones, forma ''guadalupensis'' with nearly symmetrical cones, and forma ''binata'' with intermediate cones, similar to those of the type collection of var. ''binata'' collected by Edward Palmer.<ref name="Moran1996" />

The pines of Cedros Island were previously referred to as ''[[Pinus muricata]]'', or a variety of that species described by Howell, ''P. muricata'' var. ''cedrosensis''. Other botanists, like Herbert L. Mason, instead identified it as ''Pinus remorata''. Later studies, like those conducted by [[Daniel I. Axelrod|Daniel Axelrod]], instead suggested that the pines of Cedros Island belonged to ''Pinus radiata''.<ref name="Moran1996" />

The two island varieties have two to several [[Resin canal|resin canals]] on their needles, while the mainland species has zero to two.<ref name="Moran1996" />

* '''''Pinus radiata''''' var. '''''binata''''' <small>(Engelm.) Lemmon</small> — Commonly known as the '''Guadalupe Island pine'''. Endemic to Guadalupe Island.<ref name="rebman" /> The Guadalupe pines are larger than the mainland pines, with example noted by Howell having a {{Convert|2.71|m|ft|abbr=on}} diameter trunk, greater than the largest diameter trunk recorded on the mainland of {{Convert|1.83|m|ft|abbr=on}}. The mean length of the Guadalupe Island pine's cones is {{Convert|8.2|cm|in|abbr=on}}, which is shorter than the mainland plants (measuring between {{Convert|9.6|cm|in|abbr=on}} and {{Convert|13.9|cm|in|abbr=on}}, depending on population), but longer than the Cedros Island pine's cones.<ref name="Moran1996" />
* '''''Pinus radiata''''' var. '''''cedrosensis''''' <small>(J.T. Howell) Silba</small> — Commonly known as the '''Cedros Island pine'''. Endemic to Cedros Island.<ref name="rebman" /> The mean length of Cedros Island pine's cones is {{Convert|6.5|cm|in|abbr=on}}, the smallest among all populations.<ref name="Moran1996" />

==Ecology==
[[File:Pinus radiata Lobos.jpg|thumb|right|''Pinus radiata'' forest in [[Point Lobos]], California]]
''Pinus radiata'' is adapted to cope with stand-killing fire disturbance. Its cones are [[serotiny|serotinous]], i.e. they remain closed until opened by the heat of a forest fire; the abundant seeds are then discharged to regenerate on the burned forest floor. The cones may also burst open in hot weather.<ref>{{cite book|last=Little|first=Elbert L. Jr.|year=1980|title=The Audubon Society field guide to North American trees|location=New York|publisher=Alfred A. Knopf}}</ref>

In its native range, ''P. radiata'' is associated with characteristic flora and fauna. It is the co-dominant canopy tree, together with ''[[Cupressus macrocarpa]]'', which also naturally occurs only in coastal [[Monterey County]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.globaltwitcher.com/artspec_information.asp?thingid=62524 |title=Monterey Cypress (''Cupressus macrocarpa'') |last1=Hogan |first1=C. Michael |last2=Frankis |first2=Michael P. |year=2009 |publisher=GlobalTwitcher.com |access-date=14 January 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170906035305/http://www.globaltwitcher.com/artspec_information.asp?thingid=62524 |archive-date=6 September 2017}}</ref> Furthermore, one of the pine forests in [[Monterey, California]], was the discovery site for [[Hickman's potentilla]], an endangered species. ''[[Piperia yadonii]]'', a rare species of [[orchid]], is endemic to the same pine forest adjacent to [[Pebble Beach, California|Pebble Beach]]. In its native range, ''P. radiata'' is a principal host for the dwarf [[mistletoe]] ''[[Arceuthobium littorum]]''.<ref>{{cite book |chapter-url=http://www.rmrs.nau.edu/publications/ah_709/index.html|last1=Hawksworth|first1=F.G.|first2=D.|last2=Wiens|year=1996|chapter=Dwarf mistletoes: Biology, pathology and systematics|title=Agriculture Handbook 709 |location=Washington, DC|publisher=U.S.D.A. Forest Service}}</ref>

The habitat of the pines on [[Cedros Island]] contrasts greatly with the [[Deserts and xeric shrublands|desert scrub]] on other parts of the island, forming [[Ecotone|zones]] of abrupt transition. The numerous groves form a mostly-monotypic forest of the species, with very few other plants besides seedlings emerging in the understory. In some areas, the edges of the forest form a zone that supports [[chaparral]] species, including ''[[Malosma|Malosma laurina]]'', ''[[Diplacus stellatus]]'', and the endemic ''[[Eriogonum molle]]''. With their large surfaces to [[Condensation|condense]] fog, the pines create irrigation for themselves and their associates. Towards the far northern end of the island, a [[Succulent plant|succulent]] community mostly consisting of ''[[Dudleya]]'' is found, and the endemic ''[[Dudleya pachyphytum]]'' can sometimes be found growing under the pines in the ecotone.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Oberbauer |first=Thomas A. |date=1987 |title=Floristic Analysis of Vegetation Communities on Isla de Cedros, Baja California, Mexico |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/281823533 |journal=Third California Islands Symposium |pages=115–131}}</ref>

A remnant ''P. radiata'' stand in [[Pacific Grove, California|Pacific Grove]], the [[Monarch Grove Sanctuary]], is a prime wintering habitat of the [[monarch butterfly]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Monarch Grove Sanctuary |url=http://www.pgmuseum.org/Monarchs.htm |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://archive.today/20140115004731/http://web.archive.org/web/20000925191619/www.pgmuseum.org/Monarchs.htm |archive-date= 25 September 2000 |access-date=8 September 2006 |publisher=Pacific Grove Museum of Natural History}}</ref>

In South Africa, the tree is a threat to already scarce water resources.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title = Wild Hope|last = Balmford|first = Andrew|publisher = University of Chicago Press|year = 2012}}</ref> The tree has remarkable roots.  Monterey pine roots will reach downward as far as physically permitted by subterranean conditions.  Roots have been discovered up to {{convert|12|m|sp=us}} long.{{sfn|McDonald|Laacke|1990}} Efforts to remove large quantities of the non-native tree in areas of South Africa have resulted in significant increases in accessible water.<ref name=":0" />

==Conservation status==
===Fungal disease===
The three remaining wild stands of var. ''radiata'' (Monterey pine proper) are infected and under threat of [[Local extinction|extirpation]] from pine pitch [[canker]] caused by ''[[Fusarium circinatum]]'', a fungal disease native to the southeast United States and found (in 1986) to have been introduced to California. When trees decay due to the disease, they attract bark beetles which provide a pathway for infection of other trees. In some stands, 80–90% of trees are infected. If the disease is introduced in agroforestry areas dependent upon ''P. radiata'', such as New Zealand, it could have catastrophic effects in those countries as well.<ref name="Gymnospermdatabase"/>

[[Sphaeropsis blight]] (''Diplodia pinea'') infects ''P. radiata'' in California and causes serious damage to plantations of the species in New Zealand, Australia and South Africa,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.na.fs.fed.us/spfo/pubs/fidls/diplodia/diplodiafidl.htm |title=''Diplodia'' Blight of Pines |work=Forest Insect & Disease Leaflet 161 |publisher=Northeastern Area State and Private Forestry |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161016045741/http://www.na.fs.fed.us/spfo/pubs/fidls/diplodia/diplodiafidl.htm |archive-date=16 October 2016 |access-date=5 March 2015 |url-status=live}}</ref> especially after hail damage to growing tips.{{Citation needed|date=April 2021}}

===Baja California===
[[File:Pinus radiata binata.jpg|thumb|''Pinus radiata'' var. ''binata'']]
On Guadalupe Island, var. ''binata'' is [[critically endangered]]. Most of the population was destroyed as tens of thousands of [[feral goat]]s ate ''binata'' seedlings and caused soil erosion from the mid-19th century until just a few years ago.{{when|date=January 2024}} The older trees gradually died off until by 2001–2002 the population stood at only one hundred. With a program to remove the goats essentially complete by 2005, hundreds of young Guadalupe pines have started to grow up in habitat fenced after 2001, the first significant new growth in about 150 years. Possible accidental introduction of pine pitch canker is considered the biggest threat at present to the survival of the Guadalupe Island pine population.<ref>{{cite conference |last1=Junak |first1=S |last2=Keitt |first2=B |last3=Tershy |first3=B |last4=Croll |first4=D |last5=Sánchez |first5=JA |date=13–14 November 2003 |title=Recent conservation efforts and current status of the flora of Guadalupe Island, Baja California, Mexico |url=http://www.ine.gob.mx/ueajei/publicaciones/libros/477/abstracts.html |conference=Taller sobre la Restauración y Conservación de Isla Guadalupe [Workshop on restoration and conservation of Guadalupe Island] |publisher=Instituto Nacional de Ecología |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120804024732/http://www2.ine.gob.mx/publicaciones/libros/477/abstracts.html |archive-date=2012-08-04}}</ref> The [[University of California]]'s Russell Reservation forestry research station hosts an orchard planted with 73 ''P. radiata'' seedlings from Guadalupe Island and plays an important role in conserving the ''binata'' variety.<ref>{{cite web |last=Rogers |first=Deborah L. |title=Status of Conservation of Monterey Pine |url=http://www.grcp.ucdavis.edu/publications/doc26/Chapt4.pdf |location=Davis, CA |publisher=University of California |access-date=17 March 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100610164828/http://www.grcp.ucdavis.edu/publications/doc26/Chapt4.pdf |archive-date=2010-06-10}}</ref>

==Cultivation==

===Australia===
[[File:Winter sun through trees - panoramio.jpg|thumb|Monterey Pine trees in [[Kuitpo Forest]] near [[Adelaide]] in [[South Australia]]]] 
[[File:Prospecthillforest.jpg|thumb|Monterey Pine trees plantation in [[Prospect Hill (New South Wales)|Prospect Hill, Pemulwuy]] near [[Sydney]] in [[New South Wales]]]]
''Pinus radiata'' was introduced to Australia in the 1870s.  It is "the dominant tree species in the Australian plantation estate"<ref name= Linden>{{cite web|url = https://rirdc.infoservices.com.au/downloads/05-128.pdf |title =Fauna conservation in Australian plantation forests: a review|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170808103445/https://rirdc.infoservices.com.au/downloads/05-128.pdf |archive-date=8 August 2017 |date= May 2007|first1= D.B.|last1 = Lindenmayer |first2= R.J. |last2=Hobbs}}</ref> – so much so that many Australians are concerned by the resulting loss of native wildlife habitat. The species is widely regarded as an environmental weed across southeastern and southwestern Australia<ref>{{cite web |url=https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/weeds/data/media/Html/pinus_radiata.htm |title=Pinus radiata |website=Weeds of Australia Biosecurity Queensland Edition |publisher=Queensland Government}}</ref> and the removal of individual plants beyond plantations is encouraged.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.bmcc.nsw.gov.au/sustainableliving/weedmanagement/factsheets |publisher= Blue Mountains City Council |title=Weed Fact Sheets |access-date=1 August 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150624041550/http://www.bmcc.nsw.gov.au/sustainableliving/weedmanagement/factsheets |archive-date=2015-06-24}}</ref> The [[Kuitpo Forest]], {{convert|40|km|abbr=off}} south-east of the [[Adelaide city centre]], is a planted forest of Monterey Pine trees. {{convert |30|km|mi|0|abbr=off}} west of the [[Sydney CBD|Sydney city centre]], there is a forest of introduced Monterey Pine trees in [[Prospect Hill (New South Wales)|Prospect Hill]], in the suburb of [[Pemulwuy, New South Wales|Pemulwuy]].<ref>{{cite web |url= http://weedsbluemountains.org.au/weeds/radiata-pine/ |title=Radiata Pine |website=Weeds of the Blue Mountains |access-date=8 April 2015 |publisher=Blue Mountains City Council}}</ref>

===Chile===
''Pinus radiata'' has greatly replaced the [[Valdivian temperate rain forests]], where vast plantations have been planted for timber, again displacing the native forests.<ref>{{cite web |author1=Mary T. Kalin Arroyo |author2=Adriana E. Hoffmann-J |name-list-style=amp |title=Temperate Rain Forest of Chile |url=http://botany.si.edu/projects/cpd/sa/sa45.htm |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120529120444/http://botany.si.edu/projects/cpd/sa/sa45.htm |archive-date=2012-05-29 |publisher=Smithsonian Institution}}</ref> In 2001, this species produced 5,580,724 cubic meters of lumber, or 95% of Chile's total lumber production.<ref>{{cite web |title=Douglas-fir Grown in Chile: Background |url=http://repositoriodigital.corfo.cl/bitstream/handle/11373/3075/00C7FT-09%20_Anex_5.pdf?sequence=10 |date=October 2002 |location=Concepción, CHILE}}</ref> In 2021 1.3 million of Chile's 2.3 million ha of forest plantations were planted with ''Pinus radiata''.<ref name=yearbook2021>{{Cite journal |title=Statistical Yearbook 2021 |journal=Statistical Bulletin |url=https://wef.infor.cl/publicaciones/anuario/2021/Anuario2021.pdf |last1=Daniel |first1=Soto Aguirre |date=2021-09-01 |volume=180 |last2=Gysling Caselli |first2=Janina |publisher=[[Instituto Forestal]] |trans-title= |last3=Kahler González |first3=Carlos |last4=Poblete Hernández |first4=Pamela |last5=Álvarez González |first5=Verónica |last6=Pardo Velásquez |first6=Evaristo |last7=Bañados |first7=Juan Carlos |last8=Baeza Rocha |first8=Daniela}}</ref>

===New Zealand===
The Monterey pine (always called "Radiata Pine" or ''Pinus radiata'' in New Zealand) was first introduced into New Zealand in 1859<ref>{{cite web |title=E: Pinus radiata |url=http://www.friendswbg.org.nz/downhill5a.htm |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120529120619/http://www.friendswbg.org.nz/downhill5a.htm |archive-date=2012-05-29 |access-date=7 September 2010 |website=Downhill Walk to City – Trees of Note |publisher=Friends of the Wellington Botanic Garden Inc |quote=The Acland family at Mount Peel Station had made the first NZ introduction of British seedlings in 1859...}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.teara.govt.nz/en/radiata-pine |title=Radiata pine |website=Te Ara}}</ref> and today 89% of the country's plantation forests are of this species.<ref name="Maf">{{cite web |url=http://www.maf.govt.nz/mafnet/rural-nz/statistics-and-forecasts/sonzaf/archive/sonzaf-2007.pdf |title=Situation and outlook for New Zealand agriculture and forestry |publisher=NZ Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry |year=2007 |access-date=2010-10-19 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100522144255/http://www.maf.govt.nz/mafnet/rural-nz/statistics-and-forecasts/sonzaf/archive/sonzaf-2007.pdf |archive-date=22 May 2010}}</ref> This includes the [[Kaingaroa Forest]] (on the central plateau of the North Island), which is one of the largest planted forests in the world. Mass plantings became common from 1900 in the Rotorua area where prison labour was used. In some areas (particularly areas that were formerly grazed that have had stock removed) it is considered an [[invasive species]] (termed a [[wilding conifer]] or more commonly [[wilding pine]]) where it has escaped from plantations. It is the most extensively used wood in New Zealand.{{Citation needed|date=April 2021}}

Use of pine in construction did not become widespread until forced by wartime shortages. It had been used in [[Southland, New Zealand|Southland]] from about 1920,<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/BPB19451218.2.19|title=PINUS RADIATA – UTILISATION AS BUILDING TIMBER (Bay of Plenty Beacon, 1945-12-18) |website=Papers Past |publisher=National Library of New Zealand |language=en |access-date=2017-05-05}}</ref> but doubts were being expressed about it as late as 1945,<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/AS19451215.2.60|title=FOR HOUSE BUILDING – PINUS RADIATA CONDEMNED (Auckland Star, 1945-12-15) |website=Papers Past |publisher=National Library of New Zealand |language=en |access-date=2017-05-05}}</ref> when at least one MP considered it only suitable for interior studding.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/NZH19450707.2.66 |title=PARLIAMENT IN SESSION – DAY'S DEBATE (New Zealand Herald, 1945-07-07) |website=Papers Past |publisher=National Library of New Zealand |language=en |access-date=2017-05-05}}</ref> Experiments in [[Wood preservation#Pressure processes|pressure treatment]] with water-soluble preservatives were made from 1943.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/parliamentary/AJHR1945-I.2.2.5.37|title=DEPARTMENT OF SCIENTIFIC AND INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH (NINETEENTH ANNUAL REPORT OF THE) (Appendix to the Journals of the House of Representatives, 1 January 1945) |website=Papers Past |publisher=National Library of New Zealand |language=en |access-date=2017-05-05}}</ref>

===Spain===
In the [[Iberian Peninsula]] since the nineteenth century they have been introduced mainly in the north area in order to take advantage of their wood for the manufacture of paper pulp and for shoring work in [[coal mine]]s. It is found in low altitude areas of the Autonomous Communities of [[Galicia (Spain)|Galicia]], [[Asturias]], [[Cantabria]], the [[Basque Country (autonomous community)|Basque Country]], and in the north of the [[Canary Islands]].{{Citation needed|date=April 2021}} On [[Tenerife]] the ''P. radiata'' was nearly eradicated by the 2010 [[cyclone Xynthia]].

''Pinus radiata'' forests have a negative effect on local ecology. In its plantations there are usually no other tree species, while its shady undergrowth does not allow the existence of a rich stratum of scrub. 13% of the wood cut annually in Spain comes from this pine.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.mapama.gob.es/es/desarrollo-rural/temas/politica-forestal/pradiata_tcm7-386705.pdf |title=Los pinares de pino radiata |publisher= Ministerio de Medio Ambiente. Gobierno de España|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170223214523/http://www.mapama.gob.es/es/desarrollo-rural/temas/politica-forestal/pradiata_tcm7-386705.pdf|archive-date=2017-02-23}}</ref>

===United Kingdom===
The cultivar ''P. radiata'' (Aurea Group) 'Aurea' has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref name = RHSPF>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/85554/pinus-radiata-(aurea-group)-aurea/details | title = RHS Plantfinder – ''Pinus radiata'' (Aurea Group) 'Aurea' | access-date = 30 April 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants – Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 71 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 25 April 2018}}</ref>

===United States===
''Pinus radiata'' is widely used in private gardens and public landscapes in temperate California, and similar climates around the world. It is particularly commonly grown as a landscape tree in coastal areas of California outside of its native range, where the climate is virtually identical to its native range. It is fast-growing and adaptable to a broad range of soil types and climates, though it does not tolerate temperatures below about {{convert|-15|C}}. Its fast growth makes it ideal for landscapes and forestry; in a good situation, ''P. radiata'' can reach its full height in 40 years or so. Though a combination of biotic and abiotic factors determines the natural distribution of ''P. radiata'', humans have broadly expanded its distribution up and down the California coast, even reaching [[Oregon]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=George|first=Zach St|title=The Tree That's Rare, Endangered and Common – Bay Nature Magazine|url=https://baynature.org/article/the-tree-thats-rare-endangered-and-common/|access-date=2020-11-14|website=Bay Nature|date=21 June 2020 |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Uses ==
{{More citations needed section|date=April 2021}}
[[File:Bonsai pinus radiata.jpg|thumb|Forty-five year old ''Pinus radiata'' bonsai at the National Arboretum in Canberra]]
As timber ''P. radiata'' is suitable for a wide variety of uses,<ref>[http://www.dpi.qld.gov.au/26_5424.htm "Radiata pine"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110411164816/http://www.dpi.qld.gov.au/26_5424.htm |date=11 April 2011}}, Primary Industries and Fisheries, QLD</ref> and has a resinous fragrance while being worked.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.wood-database.com/lumber-identification/softwoods/radiata-pine/|title=Radiata Pine – The Wood Database – Lumber Identification (Softwood)|website=wood-database.com|access-date=5 March 2015|archive-date=11 August 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160811093818/http://www.wood-database.com/lumber-identification/softwoods/radiata-pine|url-status=dead}}</ref> It holds screws and nails well and takes paint and stain without difficulty, and modern kiln dried timber is very easy to work.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20150126184040/http://www.nzwood.co.nz/learning-centre/radiata-pine/ "Radiata pine"], nzwood.co.nz</ref> It is about 1/3 heavier than dried [[western red cedar]]. It is brittle when bent, so does not have the same load-bearing features as Oregon pine ([[Douglas fir]], ''Pseudotsuga'').

''Pinus radiata'' is used in house construction as weatherboards, posts, beams or plywood, in fencing, retaining walls, for concrete formers. It is also used to a limited extent in boat building where untreated ply is sometimes used, but must be encased in epoxy resin to exclude moisture.

The wood is normally kiln dried to 12% moisture in {{convert|6|m|ftin|abbr=on}} long, clear lengths. It is available treated with a range of chemical salts, or untreated. Chemical salt treatment is well proven and such timber is frequently used in the ground as posts and poles as part of structures such as retaining walls and pole houses. The name applied to this treatment is tanalized wood. H1 and H2 treatment is suited to indoor use. H3 is the standard house timber and this grade is used for fence palings. H4 and H5 are the standard for inground use. In New Zealand, a 1995 change to no longer require [[wood preservation#Borate|borate treatment]] in house framing timber<ref name=NZPL>{{cite web|url=http://www.parliament.nz/NR/rdonlyres/464AB9F9-B197-4B53-BE9F-4F411CB67877/360/0210LeakyBuildings1.pdf|title=Background note: Information briefing for members of Parliament:Leaky buildings|date=6 November 2002|publisher=NZ Parliamentary Library|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121102195756/https://www.parliament.nz/NR/rdonlyres/464AB9F9-B197-4B53-BE9F-4F411CB67877/360/0210LeakyBuildings1.pdf|archive-date=2012-11-02}}</ref> was a key factor in the [[leaky homes crisis]],<ref>{{cite news|title=Leaky homes will cost $11.3b to fix – report|url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10617051|access-date=26 February 2012|newspaper=The New Zealand Herald|date=22 December 2009}}</ref> but since 2003 a series of changes have now improved the regulations.<ref>{{cite web |date=2004-05-09 |title=*ARCHIVE* – BIA Update No. 20 – Changes to Acceptable Solution B2/AS1 – Timber Durability 23 Dec 2003 |url=http://www.dbh.govt.nz/biaupdate-20 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120908232930/http://www.dbh.govt.nz/biaupdate-20 |archive-date=2012-09-08 |website=dbh.govt.nz}}</ref>

Lower grade timber is converted to pulp to make newsprint.<ref>{{cite web |title=Norske Skog Tasman |url=http://www.norskeskog.com/Business-units/Australasia/Norske-Skog-Tasman.aspx |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120906055043/http://www.norskeskog.com/Business-units/Australasia/Norske-Skog-Tasman.aspx |archive-date=2012-09-06}}</ref> Higher grade timber is used in house construction. ''P. radiata'' is used chipped to make particle board sheets, commonly used in flooring. Other sheet products are hardboard, softboard and ply. Most ply is structural and available in {{convert|7|–|22|mm|in|2|abbr=on}} sizes. A small amount of higher grade ply is used to produce thinner ({{convert|4|and|7|mm|in|2|abbr=on|disp=or}}) ply suitable for furniture, cabinet work and boat building. This is knot and crack free and glued with [[Resorcinol glue|resorcinol waterproof glue]]. Since the 1990s finger jointed joinery-grade wood has become available in up to {{convert|6|m|ftin|abbr=on}} lengths in a wide range of profiles.

In 1958, New Zealand boat designer [[Des Townson]] started building 186 cold-moulded, {{convert|11|ft|m|2|spell=in|adj=on}} [[Zephyr (dinghy)|Zephyr-class dinghies]], using ''P. radiata''. In 2011 these hand-built boats fetched very high prices, and were generally in excellent condition.{{citation needed|date=January 2023}}

The bark is used as a substrate for potting and re-potting [[orchid]]s.

''P. radiata'' is the most common species of [[Christmas tree]] in Australia and New Zealand.

In California, ''P. radiata'' is commonly planted to block wind or noise, or for ornamental uses.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Pinus radiata D|url=https://www.srs.fs.usda.gov/pubs/misc/ag_654/volume_1/pinus/radiata.htm|access-date=2020-11-24|website=srs.fs.usda.gov}}</ref>
